findings.title: Background legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
findings.body: Each asynchronous legacy operation derives its timeout context from the incoming request context. Once the API handler returns the successful unified-storage response, that parent context is normally canceled, which immediately cancels the legacy create/update/delete operation instead of allowing its intended 10-second grace period. This makes the safety copy unreliable (and often nonexistent) under normal request lifecycle timing. Start these tasks from a detached context (while retaining needed values/logging context) and apply the timeout to that context.

findings.title: Independent goroutines can apply legacy mutations out of order
findings.body: Every successful unified write launches an independent legacy-write goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a create followed immediately by an update can run the legacy update first (and fail with NotFound) and then run the create, leaving legacy with the stale initial object; similarly, delete and update operations can be reordered. Since failures are not retried, mode 3 can permanently diverge legacy from unified storage. Queue or serialize legacy mutations in request order for a resource before making them asynchronous.

findings.title: Legacy update recomputes the update against a different old object
findings.body: The same `UpdatedObjectInfo` is passed first to `Storage.Update` and later to `Legacy.Update`. `UpdatedObjectInfo` is evaluated by each storage backend against that backend's current object, so the legacy write can compute a different payload from the unified write (or fail due to different resource versions), especially after prior asynchronous lag. The previous implementation computed the update once and used an `updateWrapper` to send the unified result to legacy. Preserve that single computed object/result when scheduling the legacy update so both stores receive the same mutation.

findings.title: Mode 3 metrics attribute storage failures and legacy work to the wrong backend
findings.body: The create storage-error path records `recordLegacyDuration` rather than `recordStorageDuration`. The same misattribution exists in the update storage-error path at line 129, and the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records `recordStorageDuration` at line 166. In addition, the successful Delete storage metric at line 106 uses `name` as the kind label rather than `options.Kind`. These produce misleading error rates, durations, and high-cardinality per-object metric labels, preventing reliable monitoring of the migration.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests do not verify asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The tests return immediately after asserting the unified-storage response and never wait for the goroutine or call `AssertExpectations` on the mock. Consequently, none of the create/delete/delete-collection/update tests verifies that the legacy operation was actually invoked, received the expected object, or handled its timeout/error path. This allows broken or canceled background replication to pass the unit suite; synchronize on a channel/mock callback and assert both storage calls.
